name: The Slavic Pantheon
note: Collective grouping the principal deities of the Slavs known from the East-Slavic Primary Chronicle and the West-Slavic temple cults of Arkona, Szczecin, and Rethra.

name: Slavic Domestic and Nature Spirits
dom: household; nature; folk belief; tutelary spirits
note: Collective of lower mythological beings of East-Slavic folk belief (house, water, forest, and field spirits) documented in the ethnographic record.

name: Svetovit
note: The four-headed chief god of the great temple at Arkona on Rügen, whose white-horse oracle Saxo Grammaticus describes before the temple's destruction in 1168.

name: Triglav
note: The three-headed god of Szczecin and Wolin whose heads signified rule over heaven, earth, and the underworld, reported in the Lives of Otto of Bamberg.

name: Rugievit
note: A seven-faced war god of the Rani at Charenza (Garz) on Rügen, whose oaken idol Saxo describes being destroyed in 1168.

name: Porevit
dom: protection; war; tutelary cult of the Rani
note: A five-headed god of the Rani worshipped alongside Rugievit at Charenza on Rügen, known only from Saxo; his specific functions are unrecorded.

name: Porenut
dom: protection; tutelary cult of the Rani
note: A god of the Rani at Charenza on Rügen described by Saxo as having four faces with a fifth on his chest; his functions are unrecorded.

name: Yarovit
note: A West-Slavic war god (Latinized Gerovitus) worshipped at Wolgast and Havelberg, equated with Mars and associated with spring fertility.

name: Radegast
note: The chief god of the Redarii at the temple of Rethra, named by Helmold and Adam of Bremen; often identified by scholars with Svarozhich.

name: Zhiva
note: A goddess of the Polabian Slavs (Siwa/Živa) named by Helmold, her name connected to the Slavic root for 'living', suggesting a life/fertility function.

name: Chernobog
note: The 'black god' of the Polabian Slavs to whom Helmold says misfortune was attributed; the only securely attested member of the often-cited black/white dualism.

name: Belobog
note: RECONSTRUCTED: the 'white god' posited as a benevolent counterpart to Chernobog; not attested in any medieval source, a scholarly/toponymic inference.

name: Svarozhich
note: A fire god understood as the son of Svarog; chief deity of the temple at Rethra in the West-Slavic chronicles and the personified sacred fire in East-Slavic homilies.

name: The Rozhanitsy
note: Female birth-and-fate spirits invoked together with Rod, repeatedly condemned in medieval East-Slavic anti-pagan homilies for childbirth offerings.

name: Dola
note: The personification of an individual's allotted fate or fortune in Slavic folk belief, attached at birth; its negative counterpart is Nedola.

name: Marzanna
dom: death; winter; the dying and reborn year
note: Goddess or personification of death and winter (Morana/Morena), whose effigy is ritually drowned or burned at winter's end in Slavic seasonal custom.

name: Jarilo
note: A spring fertility figure of the seasonal folk cult whose effigy was carried and ritually 'buried', reconstructed as the dying-and-rising counterpart to Marzanna.

name: Kupala
note: The personification of the midsummer (St John's Eve) festival of fire and water; treated in some sources as a folk personification of the rite.

name: Lada
note: DISPUTED: a putative goddess of love and marriage; Brückner and later scholarship argue she is a personification mistakenly derived from a wedding-song refrain ('lado').

name: Devana
dom: the hunt; wild nature; the forest
note: A goddess of the hunt (Dziewanna) named by late-medieval Polish chroniclers (Długosz) who equated her with Diana; authenticity debated as a possible learned interpretatio.

name: Domovoi
note: The tutelary house spirit of East-Slavic folk belief, dwelling behind the stove and protecting the household and its livestock if respected.

name: Rusalka
dom: water; rivers; the unquiet drowned dead
note: A female water spirit, commonly the restless soul of a drowned or unbaptized woman, who haunts rivers and woods especially during Rusalka Week.

name: Leshy
note: The master spirit of the forest in East-Slavic belief, who guards the woodland and its animals and is known for leading travelers astray.

name: Vodyanoy
note: A malevolent male water spirit of East-Slavic folklore who rules ponds and rivers and is blamed for drownings.

name: Kikimora
note: A female household spirit associated with the stove and spinning, who troubles a disorderly home with nighttime noises.

name: Bannik
note: The spirit of the bathhouse (banya) in East-Slavic belief, who must be appeased and can scald bathers who offend him.

name: Polevik
note: A field spirit who inhabits cultivated land and may help or punish field-workers, especially those who sleep in the fields at midday.

name: Baba Yaga
dom: witchcraft; the forest; initiation; the death-threshold
note: The ambivalent witch of East-Slavic folktales who lives in a hut on hen's legs, flies in a mortar, and acts as both threat and helper to the hero.

name: Koschei the Deathless
note: An immortal sorcerer-villain of East-Slavic folktales who abducts the hero's bride and cannot die because his death is hidden in a needle inside an egg.

name: Zmey Gorynych
note: The multi-headed fire-breathing dragon of East-Slavic byliny and folktales, slain by heroes such as Dobrynya Nikitich.

name: The Finnish/Kalevala Pantheon
dom: Finnic mythology; deities and heroes of the Kalevala and Agricola's deity list
note: Collective grouping of the gods, heroes, and otherworld powers of Finnic tradition as preserved in the Kalevala and Agricola's 1551 deity list.

name: Ilmarinen
note: The eternal smith of the Kalevala who hammered out the dome of the sky and forged the Sampo, the magical mill of plenty, for Louhi of Pohjola.

name: Lemminkäinen
note: A reckless, amorous warrior-shaman of the Kalevala who is slain and dismembered at the river of Tuonela and revived by his mother.

name: Vellamo
note: Goddess of the sea and waters, wife of Ahti, who keeps the fish and is invoked by fishermen in the Kalevala.

name: Tuoni
note: Lord of the dead who rules Tuonela, the dark land of the dead reached across the river of Tuoni.

name: Tuonetar
note: Queen of the dead and consort of Tuoni, mistress of the household of Tuonela who serves the dead the drink of the underworld.

name: Kullervo
note: The doomed orphan-slave of the Kalevala whose vengeance and unwitting incest end in his suicide upon his own sword.

name: Pellervo (Sampsa)
dom: vegetation; sowing; agriculture; fertility of fields
note: Sampsa Pellervoinen, the sower-spirit of the Kalevala who scatters seed and makes the trees and crops grow over the land.

name: Nyyrikki
note: Forest god, son of Tapio, who guides hunters and marks the paths of game through the woods.

name: Tellervo
note: Maiden of the forest, daughter of Tapio, who herds and protects the cattle and game of the woodland.

name: Kalma
note: Personification of death and the stench of decay, associated with graves and the rotting corpse in Finnic tradition.

name: Hiisi
note: A malevolent forest demon (and the dangerous sacred grove it haunts), named in Agricola's deity list and the Kalevala as a source of evil and disease.

name: Surma
note: Personification of violent or sudden death, a monstrous gatekeeping power associated with the threshold of Tuonela.

name: Pellon Pekko (Pekko)
note: God of barley and the fields named in Agricola's list (Pellon Pekko), invoked for the growth of grain and the making of beer.

name: Rauni
note: An obscure figure from Agricola's list traditionally read as the consort of the thunder-god Ukko, associated with fertility and the harvest.

name: Tuonela
note: The land of the dead in Finnic cosmology, ruled by Tuoni and Tuonetar and separated from the living by the dark river of Tuoni.

name: Pohjola
dom: the far north; the otherworld; cold and darkness
note: The dark northern otherworld of the Kalevala, ruled by Louhi, where the Sampo was forged and hidden inside a copper mountain.

name: The Baltic Pantheon
dom: Baltic mythology; Lithuanian, Latvian, and Prussian deities and spirits
note: Collective grouping of the deities and spirits of the Baltic peoples (Lithuanian, Latvian, Old Prussian) as reconstructed by Gimbutas and Greimas from folklore and medieval chronicles.

name: Aušrinė / Auseklis
note: The morning star personified, Lithuanian Aušrinė (a goddess, daughter of the sun Saulė) and Latvian Auseklis (a male morning-star figure of the daina songs).

name: Ūsiņš
note: Latvian god of horses, bees, and the returning light of spring, celebrated at the festival marking the start of pasturing.

name: Bangpūtys
note: Lithuanian god of the sea and storm winds, the 'wave-blower' who raises the waves and is appeased by Baltic-coast fishermen.

name: Potrimpo
dom: rivers and waters; grain; fertility; good fortune
note: Old Prussian god of running waters and grain, one of the triad on the banner of Romuva, associated with fertility and good fortune.

name: Patulas (Pikuolis)
note: Old Prussian god of the dead and the underworld (Patulas/Pikuolis/Pecols), the third of the Romuva triad, lord of night and darkness.

name: The Mātes (the Latvian Mothers)
dom: tutelary motherhood of natural domains (forest, sea, earth, wind, fields)
note: The many Latvian 'mother' goddesses (Mātes), each presiding over a natural domain, attested in the dainas as Meža māte, Jūras māte, Zemes māte, Vēja māte, and dozens more.

name: Jūras māte (Mother of the Sea)
note: The Latvian 'Mother of the Sea', a tutelary goddess of the waters and one of the most prominent of the Mātes in the daina folk songs.

name: Aitvaras
dom: household wealth; theft of goods; fire; fortune
note: Lithuanian household serpent or flying drake that brings stolen wealth (grain, milk, gold) to the home it favors, appearing as a fiery flying creature.

name: Kaukas
dom: household; hearth; prosperity of the farm
note: Lithuanian household spirit, a small chthonic being that guards the homestead and brings prosperity if honored, named alongside the barstukai.

name: Basque Pantheon
note: Collective grouping the pre-Christian Basque mythological beings reconstructed chiefly from oral tradition by José Miguel de Barandiarán in his Mitología Vasca.

name: Mari
note: Supreme goddess of Basque mythology, lady of the mountains who dwells in caves and governs storms, hail and the weather.

name: Sugaar (Sugoi)
note: Male serpent or dragon spirit, the consort of Mari, associated with thunder and storms; also called Sugoi or Maju.

name: Mairu
note: Race of giants of Basque legend held to have built the dolmens and stone megaliths (mairubaratza).

name: Basajaun
note: The 'lord of the woods', a hairy wild-man spirit credited in legend with teaching agriculture and ironwork to humans.

name: Basandere
note: The 'lady of the woods', female counterpart of Basajaun in Basque forest mythology.

name: Gaueko
note: Genius or spirit of the night who enforces that the night belongs to him and the day to humans.

name: Eate
note: Storm and fire spirit announcing tempests and floods; sparsely attested in the Basque oral record.

name: Tartalo
note: One-eyed man-eating giant of Basque folklore, a Cyclops-type figure paralleling the Greek Polyphemus motif.

name: Lamia (Lamiak)
note: Female water spirits of rivers and springs, typically depicted with the feet of birds or fish.

name: Urtzi (Ortzi)
note: DISPUTED: the word ortzi/urtzi denotes the sky/firmament and appears in weather compounds; whether it ever named a personified sky-god is contested.

name: Sámi Pantheon
note: Collective grouping the deities and spirits of the pre-Christian Sámi noaidi religion of Fennoscandia.

name: Horagalles
note: Thunder god of the Sámi, his name derived from 'Thor-karl' (Old Thor) and widely held to be a borrowing of the Norse Thor.

name: Beaivi
note: Sun deity of the Sámi, source of light, fertility of reindeer and crops, and of mental health; gender varies across sources.

name: Mánnu
note: Personification of the moon in Sámi belief; comparatively lightly attested relative to the sun.

name: Radien-attje
note: The high creator-father of the southern Sámi cosmology, a remote sky-ruler who delegates active rule.

name: Radien-akka
dom: creation; consort of the high god
note: Female consort of Radien-attje in the southern Sámi creator-pair cosmology.

name: Máttaráhkká
note: The great mother-goddess of the Sámi who receives the soul of the child and presides over birth, mother of the three áhkká household goddesses.

name: Sáráhkká
note: Daughter of Máttaráhkká and the most venerated áhkká goddess, who aids women in menstruation and childbirth and dwells beneath the hearth.

name: Juoksáhkká
note: Daughter of Máttaráhkká, the 'bow-woman' who turns a child male and protects boys and hunters.

name: Uksáhkká
note: Daughter of Máttaráhkká, the 'door-woman' who dwells by the threshold and guards the newborn child.

name: Leib-olmai
note: The 'alder-man' or bear-and-hunt god whose favour was sought for success in the hunt, especially the bear hunt.

name: Stallo
note: Stupid, man-eating ogre of Sámi folklore who pursues humans but is regularly outwitted; a folkloric rather than cultic figure.

name: Bieggolmai
note: The 'wind-man' who governs the winds and storms with his two shovels, raising and stilling the weather.

name: Hungarian (Magyar) Pantheon
note: Collective grouping the figures of pre-Christian Magyar religion, largely a scholarly reconstruction from folklore, loanwords, and comparison since few pagan sources survive.

name: Isten
note: Supreme sky-god of the pagan Magyars whose name was retained as the ordinary Hungarian word for 'God' after Christianization.

name: Ördög
note: The adversary and spirit of the underworld and evil in Magyar belief, the dark counterpart to Isten, later identified with the Christian Devil.

name: Boldogasszony
note: Reconstructed great mother-goddess ('Blessed Lady') of the pagan Magyars, whose cult was assimilated to the Virgin Mary after Christianization.

name: Nagyboldogasszony
note: The 'Great Blessed Lady', a grand or ancestral mother-goddess of reconstructed Magyar religion, later folded into Marian veneration of the Assumption.

name: Turul
dom: origin myth; dynastic protection; the heavens
note: Mythic falcon or bird of prey of the Magyar origin myth, ancestral protector of the Árpád dynasty as recorded in the medieval chronicles.

name: Életfa / Világfa (World-Tree)
dom: axis mundi; cosmology; the three worlds
note: The 'tree of life' or 'world-tree' connecting the upper, middle, and lower worlds in reconstructed Magyar shamanic cosmology, the path of the táltos.

name: Táltos
note: Class of Magyar shaman-seers, born with bodily marks, who entered trance to journey between worlds, heal, and divine; modeled here as a collective class.

name: Hadúr
note: RECONSTRUCTED: 'War-lord' war-god, largely a 19th-century Romantic-era literary creation rather than a securely attested pagan deity.
